---
title: "Investigating Predictors of Cardiovascular Disease"
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false

## Overview

Using data from the CDC's 2024 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), this project explores how lifestyle habits—such as smoking and physical inactivity—relate to cardiovascular disease (including heart attack, angina/coronary heart disease, and stroke).

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

# Load the filtered BRFSS dataset
cvd_data <- readRDS("data/brfss_cvd.rds")

# Calculate cardiovascular disease rates by smoking status and physical activity
habit_summary <- cvd_data |>
  filter(!is.na(smoker), !is.na(exercise)) |>
  group_by(smoker, exercise) |>
  summarize(
    total = n(),
    cvd_cases = sum(cvd == "Yes"),
    rate = mean(cvd == "Yes"),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot CVD prevalence across lifestyle habits
ggplot(habit_summary, aes(x = smoker, y = rate, fill = exercise)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Prevalence of Cardiovascular Disease by Habit",
    subtitle = "Inactivity and smoking status are strongly associated with higher CVD rates",
    x = "Smoking Status",
    y = "Prevalence of Cardiovascular Disease",
    fill = "Physical Activity"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Key Findings

- **Physical Activity:** Inactive adults report nearly double the rate of cardiovascular disease compared to those who engage in regular physical activity.
- **Smoking:** Adults who currently smoke or previously smoked show substantially higher rates of cardiovascular disease than adults who have never smoked.

## The Role of Age and Cumulative Risk

Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of mortality in the United States. While lifestyle habits like smoking and inactivity are crucial modifiable risk factors, cardiovascular risk is also fundamentally shaped by non-modifiable biological factors—most prominently age. In the BRFSS dataset, cardiovascular disease prevalence climbs steadily across every age bracket, rising from just over 1% among young adults aged 18–24 to nearly 30% among adults aged 80 and older. This steep gradient reflects decades of cumulative vascular stress, plaque accumulation, and arterial stiffening.

Importantly, lifestyle behaviors and aging do not act in isolation. While chronological aging increases baseline vulnerability, regular physical exercise and tobacco cessation significantly attenuate this risk, helping older adults maintain better cardiovascular function. Disentangling how much of cardiovascular risk stems from biological aging versus preventable behavioral habits is essential for targeting public health interventions where they will have the greatest life-saving impact.
